entries.gave: Read the Cut, README.md as it stands, invoicer/lines.py and command.py: its people are accounting colleagues who save invoice lines from Excel and type one command in PowerShell with the client tax rate, writing no Python, and the developer who does the one-time pipx setup. This round adds to N9 how accounting keeps the price column free of thousands grouping in Excel and what to do when a row is refused for it, quoting the message; the rest stands.
Read readme best-practice.md N1 to N10 with template.md, and refactor-doc best-practice.md N1 to N8, before any change.
Role kept from the Cut: colleagues from accounting who bill clients from invoice lines in Excel and write no Python; inputs: the Cut names none, read to its end.
Benefit kept from the goal: print each client invoice at their tax rate yourself, without asking a developer.
What it gives kept: prints an invoice from rows saved in Excel, at the tax rate you type.
pyproject.toml read to its end: invoicer 1.5.0, requires-python >=3.9, the invoicer script at invoicer.command:main, installed by pipx.
Kind kept as a PowerShell command, the word accounting meets it by, since they type it in PowerShell.
Invoice tools readers know make a PDF, carry the client name, an invoice number and a date, offer currencies and a rate per line; kept from round 1.

Printing an invoice leads a reader to expect a file to send; covered by the no-PDF item, which says to copy the text into the letter. Prices over 1,000 with grouping are an expectation the command does not meet as typed, which the Cut settles in the everyday steps, not in Non-goals.
No closed-without-doing requests bear on invoicer in the issues; none added.

The command takes only LINES and --rate and prints EUR text, so it meets none of the four; tried in a throwaway copy, a price saved as 1,200.00 is refused naming row 1 with exit 2, and 1200.00 prints the invoice with exit 0.
Each of the four would turn away a reader who needs it, so all four are kept.
The person saw the four Non-goals in rounds 1 and 2 and asked only for the thousands grouping steps, so no question is put again.
All four kept for Non-goals; none moves to a status line.
Version 1.5.0 in pyproject.toml, above 1.0.
The use toward the goal tried in a throwaway copy: rows with a price of 1200.00 print the invoice with exit 0, and the same price saved as 1,200.00 is refused naming row 1 with exit 2.
No archived mark or notice; the developers keep it up.
Ready: 1.5.0, the use works once the price column has no grouping, and someone keeps it up; no status line.
Not carried out, as the Cut decides by user that no LICENSE file is added and the README says nothing about licensing.
Not carried out: no license is named, by the user decision in the Cut.
Not carried out: no works of others are listed, as the README says nothing about licensing, by the user decision in the Cut.
Use: accounting prints a client invoice at the client tax rate, the goal of the Cut.
Task kept: three lines, one a discount, at two tax rates, as the person asked to see a couple of rates and signed off the run in round 2.
The printed invoice with its tax and total at 19 and at 7.7 shows that the rate is theirs to set per client; what they spent is one typed command.
Cut: keep the rows, the typed command and every output line, and the refusal line exactly as PowerShell shows it; drop the usage line printed above it, which does not bear on the fix.
The one way: the rate you type for each client turns your saved rows into that client invoice.
Problem today: accounting asks a developer for each invoice at the client rate.
Doubts: are the totals right to the cent; what if a row or rate is wrong; does Excel save the rows as invoicer reads them.

The person raised prices over 1,000 saved with thousands grouping; by the Cut it is answered in the everyday steps of the Walkthrough, where accounting meets it, so How it works keeps its three doubts.
All three would change whether accounting trusts the invoice, and the walkthrough settles none of them; kept.
Answers: rounding half up to the cent and adding the printed amounts; refusing with the row named; reading semicolons and a decimal point.
Nothing is missing: each doubt has its answer in the command.
No idea is missing, so nothing is asked.
No way to make it work is missing, so nothing is handed back.
From pyproject.toml: Python 3.9 or later, and pipx install of the repository; the script name invoicer.
pipx needs Python and installs for the signed-in Windows account only, so the developer signs in as the colleague; the zip URL needs no Git.
Checks: whoami shows the colleague; py --version shows Python; invoicer --help prints its usage line.
The repository has no docs folder or changelog; its issues are on.
The issues serve help, for the developers to report a fault or ask for a change.
Help has a place, the issues, so nothing is asked.
README.md read to its end: opening, Non-goals, Requirements and Installation for the developer, Walkthrough for accounting, How it works for trust, Documentation for help.
Readers from the Cut N1: accounting, who print each invoice; the developer, who sets the command up once on each accounting machine.

Accounting knows Excel, its Format Cells dialog and File Explorer, not Python or PowerShell, and comes to print an invoice, often with prices over 1,000 shown with grouping; the developer knows py and pipx, and comes to set the command up for a colleague.

The Walkthrough keeps the once-only Excel setting apart from the steps for each invoice; the grouping fix goes in the steps for each invoice, as each invoice sheet has its own cell format, and the refusal fix right after them.
Each doubt already has its own heading under How it works; the grouping refusal is a step accounting follows, not a doubt, so it takes no heading.
The grouping fix is steps in order, so a numbered step; the refusal is a condition and its fix, so a sentence with the line PowerShell shows as a console block.
Words of the readers: the person writes thousands grouping and price column; Excel names the dialog Format Cells, the category Number, and the box Use 1000 Separator (,).
Chosen: Format Cells, Number and Use 1000 Separator (,) as Excel names them, in bold as the other Excel names; thousands grouping for what the box sets.
Facts in more than one place: the usage line, which --help shows; the refusal message, which the command prints; the decimal point, in the once-only Excel setting.
The usage line stays once in Installation; the refusal line is quoted once, in the Walkthrough, as the sign accounting matches, by the Cut decision.
No two places state a fact differently, so nothing is asked.
Names grouped: price column and column B for the one column; thousands grouping and 1000 separator for the one format; rows and lines stay two things.
Column B kept, as step 1 places the price in column B; thousands grouping kept for the format, with Use 1000 Separator (,) only as the name of the box in Excel.
Thousands separator in the once-only setting names the Excel option, not the cell format, and stays as Excel names it; no name refers to two things.

Decided: every decision of the Cut taken as it stands. Settled: a new step in the steps for each invoice, before saving, sets column B by Format Cells to Number with 2 decimal places and Use 1000 Separator (,) cleared, as Excel saves each cell as it shows it; after the steps, if PowerShell shows the refusal line, quoted as the command prints it, accounting does that step in the workbook, saves lines.csv again and types the command again. Nothing asks.
Opening kept by the template: what invoicer is and gives, then who it is for and what they achieve.
Each of the two opening sentences carries something the other lacks; none deleted.
No vague or praising word in the opening.
A developer who bills no one, or someone who keeps no lines in Excel, can tell from the opening that it is not for them.
Each kept expectation stands as a thing invoicer does not do.
The no-PDF item says to copy the text into the letter; the others have no other way.
The product is ready, so no status line is written.
Not carried out: no License section is written, by the user decision in the Cut; README.md holds no word about licensing.
Not carried out: no license link to follow, by the user decision in the Cut.
Sections in the template order, without License: opening, Non-goals, Requirements, Installation, Walkthrough, How it works, Documentation.
In the Walkthrough, the grouping step that every invoice needs sits in the steps, and the refusal fix, which only some meet, comes right after them; the list separator fix stays in How it works.
README.md read to its end as a newcomer from accounting; after step 7 the next question, what if it refuses my big price, is answered at once by the paragraph after the steps.
No answer stands before its question; nothing moved.
Each next section answers the question written; nothing added.

Run anew on invoicer 1.5.0 installed by pip from a fresh copy with an empty home folder: a price saved as 1,200.00 printed exactly the quoted refusal line with exit 2, and 1200.00 printed the invoice with exit 0; the two Walkthrough invoices are checked again in step 5.
The refusal line is a console block as PowerShell shows it, beside the rows table and the two invoice blocks.
The result first kept: At the end, you have the client invoice in PowerShell, with the tax at the rate you typed.
A colleague from accounting can say after reading that the same rows give each client invoice at the rate they type, and that a price shown as 1,200.00 must be set to 1200.00 first.
The one way kept in one sentence of the reader words: You type each client tax rate, and invoicer turns your saved rows into the invoice at that rate.
That sentence stands first in How it works, before the figure and the answers.
A newcomer reading it alone can say: I type the rate, and it makes the invoice from my rows.
The three answers kept as parts of one mechanism below the one way: read the rows, refuse a wrong one, add at the typed rate to the cent.
The figure images/how-it-works.svg kept as it stands, with each doubt beside its part; the grouping fix is a step, not a part of the mechanism.
Parts labeled in the reader words: rows, tax rate, invoice, totals.
No part has a name of invoicer own beyond the command name.
A newcomer can say back that the printed amounts add up to the total and that a wrong row prints no invoice.

Each install step is a py command the developer can copy; each everyday step says what to choose or type and where, the new step 3 by the names Excel shows: the letter B, Format Cells, Number, Decimal places, Use 1000 Separator (,).
The setup ends with the sign that invoicer --help prints its usage line in a new PowerShell window; step 3 ends with the sign that Excel shows 1200.00.
One link: the issues of lovaizu/playground, for the developers to report a fault or ask for a change.
The link is the issues URL of the public repository named in the install URL, as in rounds 1 and 2.
Headings kept: the template section names, and each doubt as the question the reader asks.
First sentences say what each section gives, such as At the end, you have the client invoice in PowerShell under Walkthrough.
Read by headings and first sentences: accounting finds the Walkthrough with its grouping step, the developer finds Requirements and Installation; neither is sent to a section they do not need.
Each new sentence has a reader, accounting: step 3 for each invoice with prices over 1,000, the condition and refusal line for when it is missed, and the fix.
No sentence marked, so no other document is looked for.
Nothing moved.
Nothing to ask.
No marked sentence to cut.
No needless words in step 3 or the refusal paragraph.
The small words kept, such as the, then and in place of.
README.md read to its end as accounting and as the developer; each still finds every step, value and condition, and no other part cites a step number that moved.
Step 3 comes after step 1, which places the prices in column B, and before saving in step 4; the refusal paragraph comes after step 7, which runs the command.
No sentence leans on anything outside the README.
Step 3 starts from the letter B, which accounting knows, and ends with what is new, 1200.00 shown and saved without grouping.
The refusal condition comes before its fix: If PowerShell shows this line in place of the invoice.
The discount as a negative price stays right after the rule of one line per row.
README.md read to its end from the top; the fix points back to steps 3 to 5 by number, which the reader has just done, so no look ahead is needed.
Step 3 is one numbered item, the steps renumbered 1 to 7.
No sequence to draw beyond the numbered steps.
The structure stays in images/how-it-works.svg.
Step 3 split into three sentences: open Format Cells; set Number without the separator; what Excel then shows and saves. The fix split from its condition.
Actors as subjects: the reader as the implied subject of each step, Excel shows and saves, PowerShell shows.
The one pronoun, it in saves it the same way, stands right after each price.
No noun made from a verb.
Objects next to their verbs: right-click the letter B, set Decimal places, clear Use 1000 Separator, save lines.csv.
README.md read to its end word by word; step 3 and the refusal paragraph read one way.
Excel names written as Excel shows them, in bold; no other word differs.
No term to define: thousands grouping is shown by its example, 1,200.00.
EUR written out at first use as euros (EUR); CSV appears as the Excel type name; no new abbreviation.
The usage line is stated once, in Installation; the refusal line once, in the Walkthrough.
No other place restates either line, so no link is needed.
Column B, thousands grouping and lines.csv written the same way in each place.

README.md Walkthrough: new step 3 in the steps for each invoice sets column B by Format Cells to Number with 2 decimal places and Use 1000 Separator (,) cleared, so Excel shows and saves 1200.00; the steps renumbered 1 to 7; after them, if PowerShell shows the quoted refusal line, accounting does step 3 again, saves lines.csv again by steps 4 and 5, and types the command again. The rest stands, with no License section and no word about licensing.

The commit check found above in step 3; rewritten as Right-click the heading of column B, which holds the prices, the words Excel users know for it. Use 1000 Separator (,) and the CSV type keep their parentheses, as Excel names them so; EUR is written out at first use.

Run in a throwaway copy with an empty home folder: this Linux machine has no py or pipx and its Python is externally managed, so the package was installed by pip --user --break-system-packages from the fresh copy; invoicer --help printed usage: invoicer [-h] --rate PERCENT LINES. The py and pipx lines on Windows were tried in round 1 from the zip and installed 1.5.0.

Tried in a throwaway copy with an empty home folder, with rows as Excel saves CSV UTF-8, a byte order mark, semicolons and CRLF: invoicer --help printed its usage line; the Walkthrough rows at --rate 19 and 7.7 printed exactly the two Walkthrough invoices with exit 0; a price saved as 1,200.00 printed exactly the quoted refusal line with exit 2; the same row saved as 1200.00, as step 3 makes Excel save it, printed the invoice with exit 0. Nothing to mend.

Made written in rounds/README.md/3/made.json: where each of the six decisions lands, no More, and eight settled points with their grounds, the new ones being the Format Cells step for column B and where the quoted refusal and its fix stand.
